original_summary: An English (ascending) auction: bidders with private valuations raise a standing bid in turn order until a full round passes with no raise. The last bidder wins and earns value minus price; everyone else earns zero. The reviewed variation made it a six-item budgeted auction with three simultaneous bidding turns per item, talk, and a rotating priority tie-break.

review.evidence: No thoughtless policy dominates. Always-pass ends on 0 and loses to anyone who buys one item below value. Always-max bids 30 on item 1, scores at most 13-30=-17 and is bankrupt for the rest of the game. However, the priority tie-break gives a built-in seat edge for N=4 (summed weights 15/17/15/13) and N=5 (20/19/18/17/16, with seat 1 also first in round 6). Ties are common because bids are small integers.

A budget of 30 against a value total of 48 forces players to choose which items to contest. Reading rivals' interest from talk and bids, and pacing the budget, separates good play from bad. The value lists are permutations of the same set, so luck of the deal is small.

Turns 1 and 2 are weakly dominated: a bid placed early commits you and leaks information, and it cannot deter anyone, because rivals can still bid standing+1 in turn 3 with no reply possible. Optimal play collapses to one sealed bid in turn 3, which removes the ascending-auction depth.
Values are private, and only the set {3,...,13} is common knowledge. Players must infer rivals' values for each item from talk and bids and plan their budget across 6 rounds.
Scores are value minus price, summed. The winner is the strictly highest score, otherwise a draw. It is pure arithmetic.
Simultaneous polls, numeric bids, private values and talk are all supported. The round fits in about 15 steps and 4 choice steps, with 6 rounds and no board.

problems: P1: The rotating priority tie-break creates a systematic seat advantage for N=4 and N=5. Integer bids make ties frequent, so the advantage matters.
P2: Bids in turns 1 and 2 are weakly dominated by waiting and sniping in turn 3. The ascending auction degenerates into a first-price sealed bid, and the early turns only duplicate the talk channel.

changes.what: Remove priority weights entirely. A turn has a winner only if exactly one player made the highest valid bid. If two or more players tie at the top, nobody wins that turn and the standing bid and leader stay as they were. A lower bid never wins because of a tie above it.
changes.why: The rule treats every seat the same in every round, for any N from 3 to 6. A tie also becomes a strategic risk, because a tied bid wins nothing, rather than a matter of seat luck.

changes.what: Add an activity rule. Turn 1 is open to everyone. In turn 2 or turn 3, a player may bid only if they made a valid bid in the previous turn, or they are the leader at the start of that turn. A player who drops out cannot return for that item.
changes.why: Waiting now forfeits the right to snipe. To contest the final turn you must enter at a binding price in earlier turns. Early bids become real commitments and signals, the field visibly narrows as in an English auction, and turn-3 bidders know exactly who they face and what those players committed.

changes.what: Record each player's eligibility in a visible yes/no attribute that is announced after each turn.
changes.why: Everyone can reason about who is still in, and the engine can enforce eligibility with a simple condition.

keeps: Ascending bidding on each item, where the leader pays their last bid and earns value minus price
Private valuations drawn from a common, known set, with every list worth the same total of 48
Six items sold one per round with a shared budget of 30, forcing a choice of which items to fight for
Simultaneous non-binding talk before each item
The strictly highest total score wins; a tie at the top is a draw

recommendation.reason: Both failures are rule-level and fixable within the limits. A seat-neutral tie rule removes the seat edge, and an activity rule restores the ascending structure.

variation.name: Budgeted English Auction with Activity Rule
variation.summary: Six items are auctioned one per round to 3 to 6 bidders with private values and a shared-size budget. Each item gets three simultaneous bidding turns. You can only keep bidding if you bid in the previous turn or are leading, and an exact tie at the top wins nothing.
variation.rules:
R1 Setup. There are N players (3 to 6). Each player starts with budget 30, score 0 and spent 0. Before round 1, each player whose values list is empty receives a private values list: a random ordering of [3,5,7,9,11,13], so every list sums to 48. A list that is already set is never overwritten. Table state starts at standing_bid 0, leader 0 (0 means no leader) and last_price 0.
R2 Privacy. A player's values list is visible only to that player. Everyone sees all budgets, scores, eligibility flags, standing_bid, leader and last_price. Everyone knows the value set is {3,5,7,9,11,13}.
R3 Items. The game has 6 rounds. In round r, item r is sold. A player's value for item r is entry r of their own list, counting from 1.
R4 Talk. At the start of each round, every player writes one short message at the same time, without seeing the others. All messages are then shown to everyone. Messages bind nobody.
R5 Round reset. After talk, set standing_bid to 0 and leader to 0, and mark every player eligible.
R6 Bidding turns. Each round has exactly 3 bidding turns. Each turn is a simultaneous poll of all players. Each player answers pass (0) or a whole number from 1 up to their current budget.
R7 Validity. A bid is valid only if all three conditions hold:
(a) the bidder is eligible for this turn;
(b) the bid is at least standing_bid + 1 (in turn 1 that means at least 1);
(c) the bid is at most the bidder's budget.
Pass, and any bid that is not valid, counts as no bid.
R8 Turn result. Find the highest valid bid.
- If exactly one player made it, standing_bid becomes that amount and leader becomes that player.
- If two or more players made it (a tie), or nobody made a valid bid, standing_bid and leader stay unchanged.
- A lower valid bid never wins.
R9 Eligibility. After each turn, a player is eligible for the next turn only if they made a valid bid in this turn (winning, tied or beaten), or they are the leader after this turn. Everyone else is marked ineligible for the rest of the round. After each turn, standing_bid, leader and all eligibility flags are announced.
R10 Resolution. After turn 3:
- If leader is not 0, the leader's budget decreases by standing_bid, their spent increases by standing_bid, and their score increases by (their value for item r) minus standing_bid. This can be negative.
- last_price is set to standing_bid. If leader is 0, the item goes unsold and last_price is 0.
- The round's result is announced.
R11 End. After round 6 the game ends. Unspent budget is worth nothing.
variation.objective: After round 6, the player with the strictly highest score wins. If two or more players share the highest score, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Waiting no longer pays, because a player who skips a turn cannot come back for that item. Players must enter in turn 1 and keep bidding to stay in, so prices rise step by step and the field narrows publicly, as in a real English auction. Entering at a low price in turn 1 is cheap, but the bid binds if nobody raises. In turn 2 a player must decide whether staying in is worth a higher committed price, knowing exactly who else is still in. Turn 3 is a final bid among known survivors whose earlier bids reveal information. The tie rule is identical for every seat. Matching a rival exactly blocks both bids, which turns ties into a risk to manage. Talk passes both tests. Players disagree because each wants items cheaply while rivals overpay or stay out, and only one player can win. A player who honours a proposal such as 'you take item 2, I take item 3' can be undercut, or can let a rival buy below value and fall behind. Simple policies all lose to sensible play: always-pass ends on 0, always-max goes bankrupt with a negative score, and always minimum-raise overpays on low-value items and runs out of budget for high-value ones.

balanced.evidence: WIN/LOSS OF THOUGHTLESS POLICIES. (a) Always pass (first option, code 0): score 0 every round, final score 0. Any opponent who buys one item below value, for example value 9 at price 4, finishes on +5 and beats it. Against random bidders it can win or draw, because random full-range bids usually produce negative scores, but against sensible play it loses. (b) Always the highest bid (whole budget): round 1, turn 1 it bids 30. It wins the item, scores at most 13-30 = -17 and has budget 0 for the rest of the game. It loses to everyone who stays at 0 or above. (c) Bid 1 in turn 1 only: it wins only unopposed items, about +3 to +12 each, and loses whenever a sensible rival bids 2 or more. It beats always-pass but does not dominate. No option is strictly better whatever the opponents do, so the payoff side is sound. A per-item table shows this: buying item r at price p yields v_r - p, so v=13 gives +13-p and v=3 gives +3-p. Budget 30 against a value total of 48 forces a choice over which items to fight for, and that is a genuine trade-off. FAILURES. (1) Seat edge from tie-breaks. Bids are small integers, so ties in turn 3 are common, and ties go to priority weight. The rotation does not divide 6 rounds evenly for N=4 or N=5. Summed priority weights over the game: N=4: seat1 4+1+2+3+4+1=15, seat2 3+4+1+2+3+4=17, seat3 2+3+4+1+2+3=15, seat4 1+2+3+4+1+2=13. N=5: seat1 5+1+2+3+4+5=20, seat2 19, seat3 18, seat4 17, seat5 16. This is a systematic seat gradient, and in N=5 seat 1 also gets top priority in the last round. Only N=3 and N=6 are symmetric. (2) Turns 1 and 2 are weakly dominated. A bid placed in turn 1 or 2 is irrevocable and does nothing that the same bid in turn 3 could not do. It cannot deter anyone, because rivals can still bid standing_bid+1 in turn 3 and nobody can respond after turn 3. It also leaks information and commits you before you see rivals' interest. The policy 'pass turns 1-2, then make one sealed bid in turn 3' therefore weakly dominates early bidding. The 'English' ascending auction collapses into a first-price sealed bid, with turns 1-2 kept only as a bluffing channel. That duplicates the talk step.

playable.evidence: Stated limits: 17 steps (max 20), 4 choice steps (talk plus 3 polls; max 4), 18 attributes (max 20), 1 hidden element (the values list), 1 random draw (dealing, once, before round 1; max 1 per round), 6 rounds (max 40). All are within limits. Every situation is covered. The validity window is explicit for each turn. A player with budget 0 can only pass. Budget can never go negative, because a bid must be at most the budget and is charged once. key = bid*10 + weight is unambiguous, since weight is at most 6, which is under 10. Priority weight is arithmetic: N - ((seat - start) mod N). Resolution, the unsold case and negative scores are all specified, and the game is finite at 6 rounds. The winner is found by comparing scores. Nothing needs a board, a clock, trades or binding agreements. Talk is simultaneous and justified: players compete for the same items, so talk can carry value bluffs and proposals for bidding rings ('I skip item 3 if you skip item 4'). Following such a proposal can cost you, and breaking it is tempting, especially in round 6. Talk is therefore something to reason about rather than something to copy. last_price is redundant but harmless.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: Every player holds the same multiset {3,5,7,9,11,13}, so total value is equal. Chance enters only through alignment: whether your high values fall on the same items as rivals' high values. For N=6, P(someone holds 13 on a given item) = 1-(5/6)^6 ≈ 0.67, so contested items are common and prices are pushed toward the second-highest value. Under good play, the deal decides perhaps 30-40% of outcomes, for example a player whose 13 and 11 face only low rival values. It does not decide the winner alone. There is substantial inference. Each list is a permutation, so a rival who bid high on item 1 has probably used up a high value, and that narrows the rest of their list. Budget levels are public. Bidding history, including spending-down, shows who can still contest later items. A reasoning player buys cheap where rivals' remaining values are likely low, saves budget for the item where they hold 13, and shades sealed bids based on rivals' budgets. A naive player overpays early or runs out of budget. Reasoning is clearly favoured.

required_changes: Remove the seat edge for N=4 and N=5. Either restrict players to 3 or 6 so that 6 rounds rotate priority evenly, or replace the priority tie-break with an arithmetic one that is seat-neutral over the game. Example: ties go to the tied bidder with the lower current score, then the lower total spent. Another option: an exact tie at the top means no valid bid wins that turn.

Make the three bidding turns a real ascending auction instead of a disguised sealed bid. Add an activity rule: a player may bid in turn 3 only if they made a valid bid in turn 1 or turn 2 (or: only the current leader and players who bid in turn 2 may bid in turn 3). Waiting then forfeits the right to snipe, and early bidding becomes a genuine commitment and signal.

balanced.evidence:
SETUP. Each player holds a private permutation of [3,5,7,9,11,13], so everyone's values total 48. Budget is 30, which is less than 33 (13+11+9), so no one can buy all their best items. Bids are simultaneous, so no seat has an edge from move order. Every player sees the same public information, so no seat has an information edge.

MAIN DECISION, one item, value v, standing bid s:
| Action | Outcome | Payoff |
|---|---|---|
| Win at s | item | v - s |
| Lose | nothing | 0 |
| Win at s > v | item | negative |
This is a first-price contest with shading, constrained by budget. No option beats the others whatever opponents do. If you bid b < v, an opponent bidding b+1 takes the item. If you bid v, your profit is 0.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES, judged by the winner rule:
- Always pass: score 0. Against sensible opponents, each sensible player wins some items below value and scores more than 0, so always-pass loses. Against random bidders, it can win, because random bidders often overpay and go negative. That is a weakness of the random opponents, not a degenerate policy: it never beats sensible play.
- Always bid full budget: bids 30 in turn 1 of round 1 and wins as the unique highest. Score is at most 13 - 30 = -17, and the budget is then 0. It loses to everyone except other overbidders.
- Always bid the minimum (standing+1): in turn 1 every such player bids 1, ties and keeps leader at 0. A sensible player who bids 2+ beats them. When it does win, it pays very little, but it is outbid by anyone with a moderate value, so it wins rarely.
- Always bid exactly your value: profit is 0 on every win. Anyone who shades and wins scores above 0, so this policy loses.
- Jump-bid v-1 in turn 1 on high values: wins at most 1-2 per item and leaves the budget unused. A shading player buying two mid items at a margin of 4-6 beats it.

No policy never loses. Both or all players can realistically win.

TIE RULE. A tied top bid blocks the item, and a lone lower bid cannot win. This adds a spoiling risk, but it is symmetric.

The auction label matches the arithmetic: a rising standing bid, the leader pays the standing bid, and value minus price is scored. This is not a cooperation game, so the 'safe option dominates late rounds' failure does not apply. In round 6, unspent budget is worthless, so bidding up to min(v, budget) is the rational play. That is intended endgame planning, not a degenerate strategy.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
WHAT CHANCE DECIDES. The deal is the only chance element, and it is equalised: every player holds the same multiset {3,...,13}. Chance decides only which rounds a player's high values collide with opponents' high values. Example: my 13 lands where the others hold 3 and 5, so I win cheaply.

WHAT REASONING ADDS.
- Inference: each player holds each value exactly once. A player who bid aggressively in round 2 has likely used their 13 or 11, so the set of values they have left shrinks round by round.
- Planning: the budget of 30 must be rationed across 6 items.
- Opponent modelling: players must judge how far to shade in simultaneous re-bids, when to jump-bid in turn 1 to shut others out through the activity rule, and whether to trust or exploit talk claims.

WHEN EVERYONE PLAYS WELL. The deal shapes the opportunities, but it does not fix the winner. Simultaneous shading and tie-spoiling decisions are mixed-strategy contests, and late-round inference about opponents' remaining values differs between players. A careless spender loses even with a favourable deal, so good play can overcome the deal.

ESTIMATE. Roughly 30-40% of outcome variance comes from deal alignment. The remainder comes from bidding and inference skill. A reasoning player is clearly favoured over a naive one, as the always-value and always-max policies show.
